TITLE: Investigating the Role of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Deformable Object Dynamics Simulation
PROPOSAL: We experiment with using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to simulate deformable object dynamics, specifically evaluating the application of a deep learning framework for forward and inverse simulation tasks, as well as its ability to handle diverse material properties and physics-based control signals.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed PINN-based approach against traditional finite element methods (FEM) and other physics-based simulators such as the Material Point Method (MPM), considering metrics like simulation speed, physical accuracy, and reproducibility.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed PINN approach may provide faster simulation speeds and improved physical accuracy, with the potential for robust handling of diverse material properties; however, potential trade-offs in accuracy may arise when dealing with highly non-linear or complex materials.

The proposed PINNs will be trained on the deformable(runtime	setState) dataset for forward simulation tasks, and the shape-net dataset for inverse tasks. We will also examine the network's sensitivity to different material parameters and evaluate its ability to generalize to unseen material properties. This experiment willlay the foundation for developing a novel physics-grounded video generation framework.

TITLE: Exploring Representations for Physics-Grounded Video Generation: Gaussian Splats and Learned Physics Priors
PROPOSAL: We investigate the use of learned physics priors and Gaussian splats as representations for physics-grounded video generation, specifically focusing on how these approaches can be used to control the video model and generate physically plausible outputs. We will compare the performance of these approaches against traditional Gaussian processes and other generative models for video synthesis.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed methods against a baseline using physics-informed neural networks (PINNS) from our previous experiment, and also include an ablation study to evaluate the effect of different physics prior learning mechanisms.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the learned physics prior approach to outperform Gaussian processes in terms of physical plausibility and efficiency, while Gaussian splats may provide better control over physics-based video generation; however, the results may be sensitive to the quality of the physics prior learning mechanism.

This experiment will use synthetic video data generated using a range of physics-based simulation tools, such as Bullet Physics and OpenMPI, and will evaluate the performance of the proposed methods using metrics such as physics fidelity, video quality, and control over dynamic physics. We will also conduct a user study to assess the perceived physical plausibility of the generated videos.

TITLE: Physics-Grounded Image-to-Video Generation with Physics-Informed Normalizing Flows
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to physics-grounded image-to-video generation using physics-informed normalizing flows (NIs), which can learn to capture complex physics-based dynamics from pixel values. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on synthetic video data and compare it against traditional video synthesis methods and physics-grounded approaches from our previous experiments.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed approach against a baseline using PINNs, Gaussian splats, and learned physics priors from our previous experiments, as well as against a method that uses a physics simulator to generate intermediate frames before video synthesis.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the physics-informed NF approach to provide better control over physics-based video generation and to be more efficient than physics simulators, while requiring less fine-tuning than PINNs; however, potential trade-offs in video quality may arise when dealing with high-quality input images and complex physics simulations.

This experiment will use the synthetic video dataset generated in our previous experiments, and will evaluate the performance of the proposed approach using metrics such as video quality, physics fidelity, and control over dynamic physics. We will also conduct a user study to assess the perceived physical plausibility of the generated videos.

TITLE: Investigating Implicit Physics Representations for Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with a multimodal encoder that fuses physics priors and visual features to guide video generation using a physics-aware, conditional GAN (Cycle-GAN or StarGAN2), where the physics priors are learned implicitly through a meta-learning setup comprising a set of diverse scene-specific physics simulators. This ensures that the video model acquires an understanding of physical laws without relying on explicit bias or prior knowledge. We will evaluate its performance on the NPF (Newtonian physics in 2D and 3D environments) purely synthetic dataset, with physics-based metrics like energy conservation, velocity consistency, and physical plausibility as the primary evaluation criteria.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) the vanilla Cycle-GAN model without physics guidance, (2) a recent, text-conditioned video generation model-independent of physics prior (e.g., TEDAN) and (3) a physics-conditioned video model where physics is explicitly modeled (physics-based simulator +  texture refiner).
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the validated physics-aware video model to match or outperform the vanilla Cycle-GAN in terms of video quality (PSNR, SSIM), and exhibit improved physical plausibility over both the text-conditioned model and the model that incorporates an explicit physics simulator, with potential robustness to varying physics settings. However, it may struggle with preserving accurate material properties and localized physics including stress, strain and material failure

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Physics Simulator Fusion for Enhanced Video Generative Models
PROPOSAL: To adapt our earlier proposal to a more robust and efficient approach, we will experiment with a heteroscedastic multi-task learning setup where multiple scene-specific physics simulators are fused into a single, unified network, with each simulator focusing on a specific kinematic regime (e.g., rigid body dynamics, soft-body dynamics, fluid dynamics). We will compare different fusion strategies (e.g., weighted averages, ensembling) and use the MT-CycleGAN (Multi-Task Cycle-GAN) framework to incorporate multiple tasks simultaneously. This will enable our model to generalize better across diverse materials and physical settings, while mitigating the effects of a single simulator's failures.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) the multimodal encoder from our initial proposal, (2) the MT-CycleGAN framework applied to a single task (e.g., rigid-body dynamics only) and (3) an ensemble method combining predictions from multiple, individually trained simulators.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By leveraging multiple simulators and fusion strategies, we expect the MT-CycleGAN framework with multi-physics simulator fusion to achieve improved performance in terms of both video quality and physical plausibility, especially for scenarios involving multiple kinematic regimes. However, it may require careful balancing of individual simulators' contributions to maintain model stability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Conditioned Graph Neural Networks for Deformable Object Dynamics
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with a physics-conditioned graph neural network (PC-GNN) that models the dynamics of deformable objects (e.g., cloth, ropes) using a graph representation of the object's mesh, where each node corresponds to a vertex on the mesh and each edge corresponds to a connection between vertices. The PC-GNN will be conditioned on physics priors (e.g., material properties, external forces) to generate realistic video sequences of deformable objects under various physics settings. We will compare different graph neural network architectures (e.g., GCN, GNN) and physics prior conditioning methods.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) a vanilla graph neural network (GNN) model without physics guidance, (2) a physics-based simulator + texture refiner for deformable object dynamics and (3) a recent, physics-aware video generation model applied to a fixed deformable object scene.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By leveraging a physics-conditioned graph neural network, we expect the model to generate more realistic video sequences of deformable objects under various physics settings, especially when compared to the vanilla GNN model. However, it may struggle with handling complex deformable object dynamics and may require careful tuning of the physics prior conditioning method.

TITLE: Revised Physics-Conditioned Graph Neural Networks for Deformable Object Dynamics
PROPOSAL: We will modify the PC-GNN model to incorporate a physics-aware temporal convolutional neural network (TCNN) architecture, which will condition the graph neural network on past dynamics and physics priors to generate more detailed and realistic deformable object video sequences. Additionally, we will incorporate a physics-aware attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant nodes and edges in the graph representation, allowing the model to better capture long-range dependencies in the object's dynamics.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) the original PC-GNN model from our earlier proposal, (2) the vanilla graph neural network (GNN) model without physics guidance and (3) a recent, physics-aware video generation model applied to a fixed deformable object scene.
COST: Estimated 350 GPU-hours (accounting for model modification and the additional complexity of the revised architecture).
PREDICTION: By incorporating a physics-aware TCNN and attention mechanism, we expect the revised PC-GNN model to generate more detailed and realistic video sequences of deformable objects under various physics settings, especially when compared to the original PC-GNN model and vanilla GNN model. However, it may require careful tuning of the model's hyperparameters to balance the effects of the additional components.

TITLE: Physics-Aware Neural Rendering for Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with a physics-aware neural rendering framework that combines the benefits of neural rendering and physics-based rendering. We will use a neural radiance field to model the object's appearance and a physics-aware scene representation to condition the radiance field on physics priors (e.g., material properties, lighting conditions). This framework will enable us to generate photorealistic videos of complex scenes with accurately simulated physics.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) a recent neural rendering model without physics guidance, (2) a physics-based rendering framework with a fixed scene representation, and (3) a generative model that jointly learns physics and rendering.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By leveraging physics-aware neural rendering, we expect the model to generate photorealistic and physically plausible video sequences, especially for complex scenes with diverse materials and lighting conditions. However, it may require careful tuning of the model's hyperparameters to balance the effects of the physics priors and the neural rendering components.

TITLE: Learning Implicit Physics Representations for Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with a learned implicit physics representation using a physics-inspired neural network architecture, such as the Physics-Inspired Neural Network (PINN) or the Surrogate-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network (SB-PINN). These models will learn a continuous representation of the physical world that can be used to guide video generation. We will compare different neural network architectures and training objectives to evaluate the effectiveness of the learned implicit physics representation.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) the multimodal encoder from our initial proposal, (2) a physics-based simulator + texture refiner, and (3) a recent, physics-aware video generation model that relies on explicit physics knowledge.
COST: Estimated 450 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By learning an implicit physics representation, we expect the model to exhibit improved performance in terms of both video quality and physical plausibility, especially for complex scenes with diverse materials and physics settings. However, it may require careful tuning of the model's hyperparameters to balance the effects of the learned physics representation and the video generation components.

TITLE: Robustness and Generalization of Physics-Guided Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the robustness and generalization of the physics-guided video generation models by applying them to diverse test scenarios with varying physics settings, materials, and object dynamics. We will also examine the model's ability to handle out-of-distribution (OOD) data, such as physically impossible or unusual situations. To improve robustness and generalization, we will explore data augmentation techniques, such as physics-based data augmentation and adversarial training.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) the physics-guided video generation models from previous proposals, (2) a recent, robust video generation model without physics guidance, and (3) a physics-based simulator + texture refiner with limited robustness and generalization.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours (primarily for data augmentation and adversarial training).
PREDICTION: By exploring robustness and generalization, we expect the physics-guided video generation models to exhibit improved performance in handling diverse test scenarios, OOD data, and physics settings. However, it may require careful tuning of the data augmentation and adversarial training Hyperparameters.

TITLE: Real-World Validation of Physics-Guided Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We will validate the physics-guided video generation models on real-world datasets and benchmarks, such as videos of everyday objects or sports, to demonstrate their practical applicability and robustness in real-world scenarios. We will also collect and label real-world data with physics annotations (e.g., object velocities, material properties) to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the models.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) recent, state-of-the-art video generation models without physics guidance, (2) a physics-based simulator + texture refiner with limited real-world validation, and (3) human-labeled ground-truth videos with physics annotations.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (primarily for data collection, labeling, and evaluation on real-world datasets).
PREDICTION: By validating the physics-guided video generation models on real-world datasets, we expect them to demonstrate improved performance in terms of video quality, physical plausibility, and robustness, especially when compared to models without physics guidance. However, it may require careful tuning of the model's hyperparameters to adapt to real-world scenarios and handling the variability of real-world data.

TITLE: Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation for Physics-Guided Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the transferability of the physics-guided video generation models to new domains and tasks by applying transfer learning and domain adaptation techniques (e.g., fine-tuning, adversarial training). We will also explore the use of physics-based common sense (e.g., generalizable physics laws) to improve the models' robustness and adaptability.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) recent, state-of-the-art video generation models without physics guidance, (2) a physics-based simulator + texture refiner with limited transferability, and (3) models that rely on explicit physics knowledge.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours (primarily for fine-tuning and adversarial training).
PREDICTION: By leveraging transfer learning and domain adaptation techniques, we expect the physics-guided video generation models to demonstrate improved performance in new domains and tasks, especially when compared to models without physics guidance. However, it may require careful tuning of the model's hyperparameters and physics-based common sense to adapt to new scenarios.

TITLE: Optimization of Physics-Guided Video Generation using Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We will apply meta-learning techniques to optimize the physics-guided video generation models for a wide range of physics tasks and scenarios. We will use a few-shot learning approach to adapt the models to new physics tasks and scenarios with limited training data. This will enable the models to learn from a diverse set of physics tasks and scenarios and generalize to unseen ones.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: (1) recent, state-of-the-art video generation models without physics guidance, (2) a physics-based simulator + texture refiner with limited adaptability, and (3) models that rely on explicit physics knowledge.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (primarily for training the meta-learning models).
PREDICTION: By leveraging meta-learning, we expect the physics-guided video generation models to exhibit improved performance in terms of adaptability, generalization, and robustness, especially when compared to models without physics guidance. However, it may require careful tuning of the model's hyperparameters and meta-learning architecture to adapt to new scenarios and physics tasks.
